title: Poulet au Yassa, Charcoal-Grilled
author: Au Sénégal
desc: A kilo of onions to a kilo and a half of chicken — the highest onion ratio in the collection — grilled over charcoal, then braised half an hour.
longDesc: Published by a Senegalese country portal under an organisation byline, and included for one reason: its onion ratio. A kilo of onions to a chicken of a kilo and a half is the most onion-forward yassa documented anywhere in this collection, and it is printed plainly. Five lemons, ten grams of chilli, one clove of garlic, five spoons of oil. The chicken marinates twenty minutes to an hour in chopped onion, garlic and lemon juice, grills over charcoal, then browns in a casserole with half the onions before water goes in for half an hour and the remaining marinade follows. The rice is steamed five to ten minutes, then cooked half an hour with the water kept level with the rice.
ingredients: 5 spoons oil — the spoon size is not printed
Salt and pepper — no quantity printed
// For the rice, per 1 kg of rice
// Water for the braise: quantity not printed
equipment: Couscoussier or steamer, for the rice
steps: Singe the cleaned and gutted chicken, cut it into pieces and place it in a dish.
Finely chop the onions and garlic over the chicken, and add the lemon juice, salt and pepper.
Remove the chicken and grill it over charcoal.
In a casserole heat the oil, add half the onions and the chicken, and brown.
Add water and cook half an hour.
Serve hot, with white rice served separately.
Bring 1.5 litres of water to the boil in a casserole and add salt to taste.
Wash the rice and steam it 5 to 10 minutes.
Pour the rice into the boiling water, keeping the water level equal to the rice level.
chefTips: A kilo of onions to a kilo and a half of chicken. That ratio is the reason this entry exists — it is the most onion-heavy documented yassa and it tells you what the dish is really about.
Keeping the water level equal to the rice level is the same instruction Senegalese cooks give everywhere, phrased slightly differently. It is the single most transferable rice tip in this collection.
Half the onions into the casserole and the rest in with the marinade at the end, so some collapse into sauce and some stay fresher.
Charcoal, by the source's own method. The grilling step is where the flavour that distinguishes a Senegalese yassa from a French onion braise comes from.
Steam the rice five to ten minutes before it goes into the boiling water. Pre-steaming is standard in Senegalese rice cookery and this source states it plainly.
Be aware this source gives NO doneness cue for any step — only elapsed times and the words brown and grill. Judge by eye and use the cues from the named-author versions at SEN013 to SEN019.
The spoon size for the five spoons of oil is not printed. Tablespoons is the reasonable reading and is offered as a reading only.
commonMistakes: Cutting the onion quantity because it looks like too much.
Flooding the rice rather than keeping the water level with it.
All the onions in at once.
Treating the absent cues as an invitation to guess at times.
sources: Adapted from 'Recette du poulet au yassa' — the H1; the page title reads 'Poulet au yassa'. Publication: Au Sénégal (au-senegal.com), path /poulet-au-yassa,3445.html. BYLINE: NO INDIVIDUAL NAMED. The recipe is credited to 'le cœur du Sénégal', which is also the publisher's own tagline — Au Sénégal, le cœur du Sénégal. SO THIS IS AN ORGANISATION BYLINE AND IS FLAGGED AS SUCH. Published 25 April 2012; last modified 28 January 2023. Yield as printed: 6 personnes. PASS STATUS: SINGLE-PASS — this entry is NOT twice-corroborated, unlike the named-author yassas in this collection.

Ingredients as printed in French: 'Un poulet de 1,5 kg'; 'Oignons : 1 kg'; 'Citrons : 5'; 'Piment : 10 gr'; 'Huile : 5 cuillères -' — PRINTED WITH A TRAILING HYPHEN AND NO SPOON SIZE SPECIFIED, reproduced as printed; 'Ail : 1 gousse'; 'Sel, poivre' with NO QUANTITY.

Method as printed, with its gaps marked: singe the cleaned and gutted chicken, cut into pieces, place in a dish; finely chop onions and garlic over the chicken, add lemon juice, salt and pepper; marinate '20 minutes to 1 hour'; remove and grill over charcoal — NO TIME, NO TEMPERATURE; heat the oil in a casserole, add half the onions and the chicken, brown — NO TIME; add water and cook 'half an hour' — THE WATER QUANTITY IS NOT PRINTED; add the remaining marinade — NO TIME; serve hot with white rice served separately.

The rice, as printed for 1 kg of rice: '1 litre et demi d'eau'; 'Sel à votre goût'; 'Riz (1 kg)'. Method: bring 1.5 litres of water to the boil, salt to taste; wash the rice and steam '5 to 10 minutes'; pour the rice into the boiling water, keeping the water level equal to the rice level; cook 'half an hour'.

A SUBSTANTIAL WEAKNESS, stated plainly: THIS SOURCE GIVES NO DONENESS CUES AT ALL. It gives elapsed times and the instructions brown and grill, but no observable endpoint for any step. That is recorded here rather than papered over, and the entry's tips point the reader to the named-author versions for cues.

WHY IT IS PUBLISHED DESPITE THAT: the 1 kg onion to 1.5 kg chicken ratio is the highest onion proportion of any yassa in this collection and it is printed unambiguously. That single figure is worth having, because the other printings leave the ratio to be inferred from weights that are not directly comparable. The entry is honest about being single-pass, organisation-bylined and cue-free.

A PUBLISHER NOTE, recorded for transparency: au-senegal.com is a Senegal country portal published by Agence Pointcom, not a tour operator, but it does carry hotel and tourism listings, and its recipe pages print no personal byline. This collection excludes tour-operator and travel-marketing recipe pages; this source sits at the boundary and is used only with the flags above attached.
healthBenefits: A kilo of onions across six servings is an exceptional source of quercetin and prebiotic fructans.
Five lemons' juice supplies substantial vitamin C.
Grilling over charcoal adds no fat.
culturalNote: A country portal publishing the national dishes under its own name is a particular kind of document — not a cook's recipe but a statement of what the dish officially is. Its kilo of onions is probably the most honest thing about it, because that is the quantity a Dakar household actually uses and most printed recipes quietly reduce.
